title: U.S. high schools using Cognitive Tutor Algebra I see a second-year gain that loses significance after correction
summary: Students using Cognitive Tutor Algebra I scored 0.21 standard deviations higher in the second year, with no statistically significant difference after correction for multiple comparisons.
account: Researchers randomly assigned 147 schools in seven U.S. states to Cognitive Tutor Algebra I or their usual curriculum during the 2007–08 and 2008–09 school years. The program combined classroom teaching, materials, and adaptive tutoring. Each year involved a new cohort of students, so no student had a second year of exposure. The revised analysis included 11,066 high-school students and 5,519 middle-school students. The researchers estimated a gain of 0.21 standard deviations for the second high-school cohort. First-year and middle-school results were not statistically significant. In its revised review, the What Works Clearinghouse found that the second-year result also failed its corrected significance threshold. Two analyses of the trial's software logs by Adam Sales and John Pane, one of them with Anita Israni, were posted in 2018, and one was published in December 2020. They found that students often left sections without showing mastery, more often in the second year, when the effect was larger. Their methods gave conflicting answers on whether hints raised or lowered posttest scores.
purpose: CTAI was built to teach first-year algebra with personalized, mastery-based software. The test-score gain is that purpose.
system: Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, with an ACT-R-based cognitive model, classroom instruction, and curriculum materials
deployer: Participating public and Catholic parochial schools in 51 districts across seven states (study sites)

ratings.reason: The second high-school cohort had a measurable algebra gain, although the corrected significance test was inconclusive.

ai_role.statement: The tutor provided adaptive exercises, hints and mastery-based progression within a complete algebra curriculum. The trial did not separate its contribution from classroom teaching, materials or training. Later analyses of the trial's software logs by Adam Sales, John Pane and Anita Israni gave conflicting answers on whether hint use helped. They also found that students often moved on without mastery, and more often in the second year, when the effect was larger.

source_inspections.title: Original authors’ supplemental analysis
source_inspections.contribution: The authors’ alternative analysis excludes study joiners and uses actual pretest scores. Their preferred model estimates a second-cohort high-school effect of 0.21 standard deviations with an unadjusted p-value of .04.
source_inspections.locator: RAND working paper, Methods and Results of Supplemental Analysis, Tables 1–4, especially Table 3.
source_inspections.access_status: The direct cached retrieval returned 403. The Methods, results, and tables were read through the public web-tool extraction of the RAND PDF.

source_inspections.title: Independent evidence review
source_inspections.contribution: WWC applies a multiple-comparison correction with a critical p-value of .025 and classifies the second-cohort result as statistically inconclusive. Its review excludes the middle-school results because baseline equivalence was not demonstrated.
source_inspections.locator: WWC intervention report, algebra-domain summary on page 6 and Appendix C.1, pages 30–31, note c for Pane et al. (2014).
source_inspections.access_status: The specified passages were read in saved public-source text.

latest_review.limitations: The intervention includes classroom instruction and curriculum materials, so the estimate does not isolate the software.

data.scope: The listed original sources or intermediaries were inspected for the identified claims. Access limits remain explicit.
data.ordering_basis: The existing lead supports the central case account. Additional material records the original evidence and its qualifications; source independence is assessed separately.

display.answer: The 2014 trial paper and its RAND addendum provide the estimates, and the What Works Clearinghouse review supplies the correction for multiple comparisons. The analyses of the trial's software logs by Sales, Pane and Israni draw on the same trial, and Pane is also an author of the trial paper.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.
